opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the main thing was really about building culture and visibility from day one. When you're starting a new team in a new location, there's always this risk that people feel like they're a satellite office, a bit disconnected from where the "real" work is happening. I didn't want that at all. I wanted the folks here to feel like they're plugged directly into the core of Gemini, not on the periphery.

Having Jeff and Quoc come out was a very strong signal of that, both internally and externally. Internally, it tells the team that leadership cares about what we're doing here and that this is a serious investment. Externally, it helps put Singapore on the map as a place where frontier AI research actually happens. Historically, a lot of really talented people in this region felt like they had to move to the Bay Area or London to work on the most cutting-edge stuff, and I want to change that perception.

The other part was simply inspiration and talent. Jeff and Quoc are people who've shaped the field for over a decade. Getting students, researchers, and engineers in the room with them, letting them hear how these folks think about problems, about research taste, about scaling, that has a lasting effect. Some of the best hires come from moments like that, where someone walks out thinking, "I want to be part of this."

So for me it was a mix of things: kickstart the team's identity, make it clear we're doing core work, and build a community and talent pipeline around Gemini here in Singapore. It's a long game, but you have to plant the flag early.

r001.rationale: Calling it “a long game” and describing the symposium as an early step to build identity, community, and a talent pipeline characterizes team formation as ongoing rather than a single launch moment.

r002.rationale: The response says Singapore should be seen as a place where “frontier AI research actually happens” and aims to change the perception that people must leave the region to work on cutting-edge research.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the main thing I wanted was for the team to feel like they were part of Gemini, not some satellite office. When you're setting up a new site far from Mountain View, the biggest risk isn't talent or compute, it's that people feel disconnected from where the actual decisions get made. So having Jeff and Quoc physically there, talking about the roadmap, answering questions directly, that does a lot more than any number of video calls. It signals to the team, and frankly to the broader Singapore ecosystem, that this is real.

The second thing was more practical. A lot of the folks we hired in Singapore are extremely strong but hadn't worked at the frontier before, so there's a gap between knowing the papers and knowing how things actually get done inside a big pretraining effort. I wanted them to hear from Jeff and Quoc what matters and what doesn't, what the taste is, how you think about scaling, how you prioritize when everything looks promising. That kind of context is hard to transmit through docs.

And then selfishly, I wanted to put a flag down. Singapore has a lot of good people who historically ended up leaving for the US or just not working on this stuff at all. I think showing that you can do frontier work from here, with the same people and the same stakes, changes who decides to stay. If a few more people end up doing serious research in the region because of that week, I'd consider it a success.

r001.rationale: The response describes setting up a new Singapore site and holding a symposium, but does not characterize forming the team as gradual rather than a single launch moment.

r002.rationale: The response says frontier work can be done from Singapore with the same people and stakes, expressing confidence that Singapore can be close to the AI frontier.
